title: "Officiating, Replay, and the Rules of the Ball"
subtitle: "Seven officials, three ways into the replay booth, and the handful of rules that decide who has the ball, so you can call it before the referee turns on his microphone."
description: "The seven-person NFL officiating crew (referee, umpire, down judge, line judge, side judge, field judge, back judge): where each one stands and what each one watches. Replay in three doors: the coach's challenge (two, plus a third if either succeeds, since 2024), booth review (scoring plays, turnovers, tries, fourth-down spots short of the line and everything after the two-minute warning) and replay assist (since 2021; its power to overturn certain flags, added in 2024 and widened in 2025; the 2026 consult on ejections), and why there is still no sky judge. The rules of the ball: the 2018 catch rule and the plays that forced it, down by contact, forward progress, fumble versus incomplete pass, the fumble through the end zone, backward versus forward passes, and intentional grounding and the tackle box. How to read a referee's announcement, the 2025 Hawk-Eye virtual measurement, and what nflverse data says about replay and about crews."
glossary:
  "Referee": "The crew chief of the seven NFL officials, the only one in a white cap. He stands 10 to 12 yards behind the line in the offensive backfield, on the side of the quarterback's throwing arm, watches the quarterback and hits on him, rules on the quarterback's fumbles and passes, and announces every foul and replay result over his microphone."
  "Umpire": "The official responsible for the interior line: holding, false starts and illegal hands among the center, guards and the defenders across from them. Since 2010 he stands in the offensive backfield, opposite the referee; he also spots the ball after most plays and checks equipment."
  "Down judge": "The official who straddles the line of scrimmage on one sideline (the side with the chain crew). He rules on offside, encroachment, false starts and illegal formations on his side, watches the receivers and the sideline nearest him, marks forward progress and runs the chain crew. Called the head linesman until 2017."
  "Line judge": "The official who straddles the line of scrimmage on the sideline opposite the down judge, with the same duties on his side: offside, false starts, illegal formation, the near receivers and sideline, forward progress, and whether a pass was thrown from beyond the line."
  "Side judge": "The deep official on the down judge's side, about 20 yards past the line near the sideline. He watches the receivers on his side for pass interference, illegal contact and holding, and rules on catches and out of bounds near his sideline."
  "Field judge": "The deep official on the line judge's side, about 20 yards past the line near the sideline, with the same job as the side judge on that half of the field. On field goals he stands under one upright."
  "Back judge": "The deepest official, about 25 yards past the line in the middle of the field. He watches the tight end and inside receivers, the deep middle and the end line, and stands under the other upright on field goals."
  "Coach's challenge": "A head coach's request, made by throwing a red flag before the next snap, for a replay review of a reviewable ruling. Each team gets two per game, plus a third if either of the first two succeeds (since 2024); a team must have a timeout to challenge and loses it if the challenge fails. Not allowed inside the final two minutes of a half or in overtime, where the booth reviews instead."
  "Replay review": "Checking an on-field ruling against video. The ruling is reversed only if the video shows clear and obvious evidence that it was wrong; otherwise it 'stands' (not enough evidence either way) or is 'confirmed' (the video supports it). Since 2017 the final decision in the NFL is made in New York, by the league's senior vice president of officiating or a designee, consulting the replay official and the referee."
  "Booth review": "A replay review started by the replay official in the stadium (or the officiating command center in New York), not by a coach. It covers every scoring play, every turnover, every try, every ruling that the offense came up short on fourth down, and reviewable plays after the two-minute warning of each half and in overtime. A coach may not challenge these."
  "Replay assist": "The replay booth's quick help to the on-field crew, before the next snap and usually with no stoppage, on clear-cut objective facts (possession, the spot relative to a line, whether a pass was caught, whether a player was down or out of bounds, the clock), used since 2021. Since 2024 it may also wipe out certain flags when clear video shows the objective element of the foul didn't happen (no contact with the passer's head or neck on roughing the passer, the passer outside the pocket on grounding, the runner still in bounds on a late hit, from 2024; face mask, horse-collar, tripping, hits to a defenseless player's head or neck and roughing or running into the kicker added in 2025), but it cannot add a foul nobody called. Since 2026 league officiating staff may also consult on ejections for flagrant acts."
  "Catch (completed pass)": "Under the rule rewritten in 2018, a player catches a forward pass when he (1) secures control of the ball in his hands or arms before it touches the ground, (2) touches the ground in bounds with both feet or another body part other than his hands, and then (3) makes an act common to the game, such as tucking the ball, turning upfield or reaching for the line, or keeps control long enough to do so. The same test decides an interception."
  "Forward progress": "The farthest point toward the opponent's goal that the ball reached before the ball carrier was stopped. The ball is spotted there, not where he ended up after being driven back, and officials blow the play dead once his progress is stopped."
  "Down by contact": "The NFL's rule for ending a run: the ball carrier is down when any part of his body other than his hands or feet touches the ground after he has been touched by an opponent. Contact can come first or second: a runner who slips untouched may get up and keep going, but if an opponent touches him while he is on the ground, he is down (in college he is down when his knee hits, touched or not)."
  "Fumble through the end zone (touchback)": "A fumble that goes forward into the opponent's end zone and out of bounds there (out the side or the back). The offense loses the ball even though nobody recovered it: it is a touchback, and the defense takes over at its own 20."
  "Backward pass": {def: "Any pass that is not forward, including one thrown straight across the field parallel to the line. Anyone may throw one at any time, from anywhere; if it hits the ground the ball is still live, so either team may recover it, and advance it.", aliases: ["Lateral"]}
  "Intentional grounding": "A foul by a passer who, facing an imminent loss of yardage, throws a pass that isn't in the direction and vicinity of an eligible receiver. It costs a loss of down and 10 yards (or the spot of the pass, if that is worse), and a safety if he throws it from his own end zone. A passer who is or has been outside the tackle box may throw it away freely if the ball reaches the line of scrimmage."
  "Tackle box": "The area between the outside edges of where the two offensive tackles lined up, from the line of scrimmage back to the offense's own end line; in the rulebook, the 'pocket area'. Inside it, a throwaway must go near an eligible receiver; once the passer, or the ball, has been outside it, a throwaway only has to reach the line of scrimmage."
  "Virtual measurement": {def: "The NFL's camera-based first-down measurement, used since 2025: a Sony Hawk-Eye system of six 8K cameras in every stadium measures from the officials' spot of the ball to the line to gain, in place of the chain crew walking onto the field. The officials still spot the ball by eye, and the chains stay on the sideline as a backup.", aliases: ["Hawk-Eye measurement"]}

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (drawing helpers for this chapter)"}
import logging
import os
import shutil

import numpy as np
import pandas as pd
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt
from matplotlib import animation
from matplotlib.lines import Line2D
from matplotlib.patches import Circle, Ellipse, FancyArrowPatch, FancyBboxPatch, Polygon, Rectangle
from IPython.display import HTML, Markdown, display

from gridiron import Play, Player, Field, offense, defense, routes as r, style, draw_marker, draw_frame
from gridiron.field import FIELD_WIDTH, HASH_NEAR, HASH_FAR, MIDDLE

logging.getLogger("matplotlib.font_manager").setLevel(logging.ERROR)
style.apply()
PDF = os.environ.get("RTG_FORMAT", "").lower() in ("pdf", "typst", "print")
GREEN = "#0f7a55"            # darker step of the aqua highlight: "legal" on the light field
RED = style.SERIES[7]        # "foul"
PURPLE = style.SERIES[6]     # the tackle box
ZEBRA = style.INK            # officials: white disc, black ring
BOX_W = 2 * 1.6 + 0.8        # outside edge of a tackle's normal position, yards from the ball


def O(key, pos, d, w, label=""):
    """An offensive (blue) player at (d, w): d = yards downfield of the line, w = yards to the offense's right."""
    return Player(key, pos, "off", d, w, label=label)


def D(key, pos, d, w, label=""):
    """A defensive (orange) player."""
    return Player(key, pos, "def", d, w, label=label)


def XY(fld, p, d, w):
    """(d, w) in the offense's frame -> plot coordinates on a drawn field."""
    x, y = fld.xy(*p.to_abs(d, w))
    return float(x), float(y)


def say(fld, p, d, w, text, color=style.INK_2, fs=6.8, ha="center", weight="normal", box=True, rot=0):
    """A short on-field label at (d, w), on a light pad so lines underneath don't cut it."""
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    kw = dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.18", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none", alpha=0.92) if box else None
    fld.ax.text(x, y, text, fontsize=fs, color=color, ha=ha, va="center", zorder=12, fontweight=weight,
                linespacing=1.12, bbox=kw, rotation=rot)


def path_arrow(fld, p, pts, color=style.BALL, lw=1.4, ls=(0, (2.5, 2)), head=9, z=7, rad=0.0):
    """A dashed arrow through (d, w) points: a ball's flight or a loose ball's bounce."""
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in pts]
    if len(xy) > 2:
        xs, ys = zip(*xy[:-1])
        fld.ax.plot(xs, ys, color=color, lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z)
    fld.ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(xy[-2], xy[-1], arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=head, color=color,
                                     lw=lw, ls=ls, zorder=z, connectionstyle=f"arc3,rad={rad}"))


def xmark(fld, p, d, w, color=style.DEFENSE_DARK, ms=8):
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    fld.ax.plot(x, y, marker="x", ms=ms, mew=2.2, color=color, zorder=11)


def ball_at(fld, p, d, w):
    x, y = XY(fld, p, d, w)
    draw_marker(fld.ax, x, y, "ball", "", fld.pts_per_yard())


def no_numbers(ax):
    """Drop the painted yard numbers: on zoomed diagrams they compete with the labels."""
    for t in list(ax.texts):
        if t.get_text().isdigit():
            t.remove()


def official(ax, x, y, label, ppy, r=1.1, alpha=1.0):
    """An official: white disc with a black ring (offense = blue disc, defense = orange square)."""
    ax.add_patch(Circle((x, y), r, fc="white", ec=ZEBRA, lw=1.6, zorder=9, alpha=alpha))
    fs = max(4.6, min(8.5, r * ppy * (1.15 if len(label) == 1 else 0.92)))
    ax.text(x, y, label, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=fs, color=ZEBRA, fontweight="bold", zorder=10,
            alpha=alpha)


def marker_legend(ax, y=-0.01, extra=()):
    h = [Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor=style.OFFENSE, markeredgecolor="white", ms=8,
                label="Offense"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="D", ls="", markerfacecolor=style.DEFENSE_TINT, markeredgecolor=style.DEFENSE,
                ms=7, label="Defense"),
         Line2D([], [], marker="o", ls="", markerfacecolor="white", markeredgecolor=ZEBRA, mew=1.6, ms=9,
                label="Official")] + list(extra)
    ax.legend(handles=h, loc="upper center", bbox_to_anchor=(0.5, y), ncol=len(h), fontsize=7.2,
              frameon=False, handletextpad=0.4, columnspacing=1.2)


def tackle_box(ax, fld, p, back, alpha=0.10):
    """The shaded tackle box (the rulebook's pocket area), from the line back to depth `back`."""
    xy = [XY(fld, p, *q) for q in [(-0.7, -BOX_W), (-0.7, BOX_W), (back, BOX_W), (back, -BOX_W)]]
    ax.add_patch(Polygon(xy, closed=True, fc=PURPLE, alpha=alpha, ec=PURPLE, lw=0.9, ls=(0, (3, 2)),
                         zorder=1.4))


# --- flowchart pieces ---------------------------------------------------------------------------
def fbox(ax, x, y, w, h, title, body="", fc=style.SURFACE, ec=style.BASELINE, tfs=7.8, bfs=6.7, lw=1.0):
    ax.add_patch(FancyBboxPatch((x - w / 2, y - h / 2), w, h, boxstyle="round,pad=0.02,rounding_size=1.1",
                                fc=fc, ec=ec, lw=lw, zorder=3))
    if body:
        ax.text(x, y + h / 2 - 1.6, title, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=tfs, fontweight="bold",
                color=style.INK, zorder=4, linespacing=1.1)
        nl = title.count("\n") + 1
        ax.text(x, y + h / 2 - 1.9 - 2.9 * nl, body, ha="center", va="top", fontsize=bfs, color=style.INK_2,
                zorder=4, linespacing=1.18)
    else:
        ax.text(x, y, title, ha="center", va="center", fontsize=tfs, fontweight="bold", color=style.INK,
                zorder=4, linespacing=1.15)


def farrow(ax, p0, p1, text=None, color=style.INK_2, toff=(0.0, 0.0), ha="center", fs=6.8):
    ax.add_patch(FancyArrowPatch(p0, p1, arrowstyle="-|>", mutation_scale=10, color=color, lw=1.0,
                                 shrinkA=1, shrinkB=1, zorder=2))
    if text:
        ax.text((p0[0] + p1[0]) / 2 + toff[0], (p0[1] + p1[1]) / 2 + toff[1], text, ha=ha, va="center",
                fontsize=fs, color=color, fontweight="bold", zorder=5,
                bbox=dict(boxstyle="round,pad=0.12", fc=style.SURFACE, ec="none"))


def canvas(w_in, h_in, xmax=100, ymax=None):
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(w_in, h_in))
    ymax = ymax or xmax * h_in / w_in
    ax.set_xlim(0, xmax); ax.set_ylim(0, ymax); ax.set_axis_off(); ax.grid(False)
    return fig, ax


# --- scenes: simulated tracking plus extra actors (officials), as a video or a frame strip ------
def kf_interp(kf, t):
    kf = np.asarray(kf, dtype=float)
    return np.array([np.interp(t, kf[:, 0], kf[:, 1]), np.interp(t, kf[:, 0], kf[:, 2])])


def draw_scene(ax, play, trk, t, window, lateral, extra=None, decor=None, trails=True, clock=True):
    """One moment of a play on `ax`: players (and ball) from tracking `trk`, extra actors from keyframes."""
    ylo, yhi = sorted((play.ball_y - lateral[1], play.ball_y - lateral[0]))
    fld = Field(ax=ax, orient="vertical", los=play.los, window=window, to_go=play.to_go, lateral=(ylo, yhi))
    no_numbers(ax)
    ppy = fld.pts_per_yard()
    if decor:
        decor(fld, t)
    times = trk.groupby("frameId")["time"].first()
    fid = int((times - t).abs().idxmin())
    cur = trk[trk.frameId == fid]
    hist = trk[trk.frameId <= fid] if trails else None
    draw_frame(fld, cur, hist, ppy)
    for key, (lab, kf) in (extra or {}).items():
        ts = np.linspace(min(np.asarray(kf)[:, 0].min(), 0), t, 30)
        pts = np.array([kf_interp(kf, s) for s in ts])
        xs, ys = zip(*[XY(fld, play, d, w) for d, w in pts])
        if trails:
            ax.plot(xs, ys, color=ZEBRA, lw=0.9, alpha=0.35, zorder=3)
        official(ax, xs[-1], ys[-1], lab, ppy, r=1.15)
    for art in list(ax.patches) + list(ax.texts) + list(ax.lines):
        art.set_clip_on(True)                   # players who ran out of the window don't spill outside it
    if clock:
        ax.set_title("snap" if abs(t) < 1e-6 else f"{t:+.1f} s", fontsize=8.6, color=style.INK_2)
    return fld


def show_scene(play, trk, times, window, lateral, extra=None, decor=None, notes=None, ncols=2, width_in=6.5):
    """HTML: a video of the scene. PDF: a frame strip at `times`, each panel with its note."""
    trk = trk.copy()
    trk["_id"] = trk["displayName"].astype(str)
    if PDF:
        n = len(times)
        nrows = int(np.ceil(n / ncols))
        span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
        pw = width_in / ncols
        fig, axes = plt.subplots(nrows, ncols, figsize=(width_in, nrows * (pw * span_d / span_w + 0.35)),
                                 squeeze=False)
        for ax in axes.flat[n:]:
            ax.axis("off")
        for i, (ax, t) in enumerate(zip(axes.flat, times)):
            fld = draw_scene(ax, play, trk, t, window, lateral, extra, decor)
            if notes:
                notes(fld, i, t)
        fig.tight_layout(h_pad=1.0, w_pad=0.6)
        plt.show()
        return
    tmax = float(trk["time"].max())
    t0 = float(trk["time"].min())
    ts = np.round(np.arange(max(t0, -0.5), tmax + 1e-9, 0.1), 2)
    span_w, span_d = lateral[1] - lateral[0], window[1] - window[0]
    fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(5.6, 5.6 * span_d / span_w))
    hold = {}

    def update(t):
        ax.clear()
        fld = draw_scene(ax, play, trk, float(t), window, lateral, extra, decor)
        if notes:
            # show the note of the last panel time already passed
            k = max([i for i, tt in enumerate(times) if tt <= t + 1e-6] or [0])
            notes(fld, k, float(t))
        return []

    anim = animation.FuncAnimation(fig, update, frames=ts, interval=100, blit=False)
    if shutil.which("ffmpeg"):
        html = anim.to_html5_video(embed_limit=40).replace("<video ", '<video style="max-width:100%;height:auto" ')
    else:
        html = anim.to_jshtml(default_mode="once")
    plt.close(fig)
    display(HTML(html))


def md_table(rows, header, align):
    lines = ["| " + " | ".join(header) + " |", "|" + "|".join(align) + "|"]
    lines += ["| " + " | ".join(map(str, row)) + " |" for row in rows]
    return Markdown("\n".join(lines))
```

``` {.python .cell-code code-summary="Show the Python (load officials, penalties and replay reviews from nflverse)"}
import re
from gridiron.data import nfl, pbp

SEASONS = list(range(2016, 2026))     # 2016-2025, the last ten completed seasons
cols = ["game_id", "old_game_id", "season", "season_type", "penalty", "desc", "replay_or_challenge"]
raw = pbp(SEASONS, columns=cols)
raw["desc"] = raw["desc"].fillna("")
S = {}                                # numbers quoted in the text

# --- accepted penalties per game, by the referee who led the crew -------------------------------
# nflverse play text writes an accepted foul as "PENALTY on ..." and a declined or offsetting one as
# "Penalty on ...", so counting the capitalised form counts accepted fouls (both teams, every play).
raw["accepted"] = raw["desc"].str.count("PENALTY on")
games = raw.groupby(["old_game_id", "season", "season_type"], as_index=False)["accepted"].sum()
offs = nfl().load_officials().to_pandas()
refs = (offs[offs.position == "Referee"][["game_id", "season", "official_name"]]
        .rename(columns={"game_id": "old_game_id", "official_name": "referee"}))
games = games.merge(refs, on=["old_game_id", "season"], how="left")
reg = games[games.season_type == "REG"]
by_season = reg.groupby("season")["accepted"].mean()
crew = (reg[reg.season.isin([2024, 2025])].groupby(["referee", "season"])["accepted"]
        .agg(["mean", "size"]).reset_index())
wide = crew.pivot(index="referee", columns="season", values="mean").dropna().sort_values(2025)
n25 = crew[crew.season == 2025].set_index("referee")["size"].reindex(wide.index)
avg25 = reg[reg.season == 2025]["accepted"].mean()
sd_game = reg[reg.season == 2025]["accepted"].std()
se_crew = sd_game / np.sqrt(n25.mean())
S["pen25"] = f"{avg25:.1f}"
S["pen24"] = f"{by_season[2024]:.1f}"
S["pen_lo"], S["pen_hi"] = f"{by_season.min():.1f}", f"{by_season.max():.1f}"
S["crew_lo"], S["crew_hi"] = f"{wide[2025].min():.1f}", f"{wide[2025].max():.1f}"
S["crew_lo_name"], S["crew_hi_name"] = wide[2025].idxmin(), wide[2025].idxmax()
S["sd_game"] = f"{sd_game:.1f}"
S["se2"] = f"{2 * se_crew:.1f}"
S["ncrew"] = f"{len(wide)}"
S["r2425"] = f"{wide[2024].corr(wide[2025]):.2f}"
yy = []
cc = reg.groupby(["referee", "season"])["accepted"].mean().unstack()
for y in range(2016, 2025):
    d = cc[[y, y + 1]].dropna()
    yy.append(d[y].corr(d[y + 1]))
S["r_lo"], S["r_hi"] = f"{min(yy):.2f}", f"{max(yy):.2f}"
S["r_med"] = f"{np.median(yy):.2f}"
# share of crews whose 2024 rank half (top or bottom eight) held in 2025
top24 = wide[2024] > wide[2024].median()
top25 = wide[2025] > wide[2025].median()
S["same_half"] = f"{(top24 == top25).sum()}"
# the same question for teams: does a team's own accepted-foul rate hold from one season to the next?
regp = raw[raw.season_type == "REG"]
tf = regp.assign(tm=regp["desc"].str.findall(r"PENALTY on ([A-Z]{2,3})-")).explode("tm").dropna(subset=["tm"])
tcount = tf.groupby(["season", "tm"]).size().unstack(0)
team_rate = tcount.apply(lambda c: c / (16 if c.name <= 2020 else 17))     # games per team
tyy = [team_rate[[y, y + 1]].dropna().corr().iloc[0, 1] for y in range(2016, 2025)]
S["team_r_med"] = f"{np.median(tyy):.2f}"

# --- replay reviews written into the play-by-play -----------------------------------------------
rv = raw[raw.replay_or_challenge == 1].copy()
ex = rv["desc"].str.extract(r"(challenged|Replay Official reviewed|Replay Assistant challenged|reviewed) "
                            r"the (.*?) ruling, and the play was (\w+)")
rv["who"] = np.where(ex[0].eq("challenged"), "challenge", np.where(ex[0].notna(), "booth", None))
rv["what"], rv["result"] = ex[1], ex[2].str.lower()
rv = rv[rv.who.notna()]
rv["reversed"] = rv["result"].eq("reversed")
ch = rv[(rv.who == "challenge") & (rv.season_type == "REG")]
ngames = raw[raw.season_type == "REG"].groupby("season")["game_id"].nunique()
S["ch_rate"] = f"{100 * ch.reversed.mean():.0f}%"
S["ch_rate24"] = f"{100 * ch[ch.season == 2024].reversed.mean():.0f}%"
S["ch_rate25"] = f"{100 * ch[ch.season == 2025].reversed.mean():.0f}%"
S["ch_pg25"] = f"{len(ch[ch.season == 2025]) / ngames[2025] / 2:.2f}"
S["ch_n25"] = f"{len(ch[ch.season == 2025])}"
S["g25"] = f"{ngames[2025]}"
recent = rv[rv.season.between(2021, 2025)]
S["rv_n"] = f"{len(recent):,}"
LABELS = {"pass completion": "Ruled a catch", "incomplete pass": "Ruled incomplete",
          "runner broke the plane": "Ruled a touchdown (broke the plane)",
          "short of the line to gain": "Spot: short of the line to gain", "first down": "Spot: ruled a first down",
          "fumble": "Ruled a fumble", "runner was not down by contact": "Ruled not down by contact",
          "interception": "Ruled an interception", "runner was down by contact": "Ruled down by contact",
          "short of the goal line": "Ruled short of the goal line",
          "runner was inbounds": "Ruled in bounds", "runner was out of bounds": "Ruled out of bounds"}
tab = (recent[recent.what.isin(LABELS)].groupby(["what", "who"]).size().unstack(fill_value=0))
tab["n"] = tab.sum(axis=1)
tab["rev"] = recent[recent.what.isin(LABELS)].groupby("what")["reversed"].mean()
tab = tab.sort_values("n")
S["catch_share"] = f"{100 * (tab.loc[['pass completion', 'incomplete pass'], 'n'].sum()) / len(recent):.0f}%"
S["plane_rev"] = f"{100 * tab.loc['runner broke the plane', 'rev']:.0f}%"
S["incomp_rev"] = f"{100 * tab.loc['incomplete pass', 'rev']:.0f}%"
S["catch_rev"] = f"{100 * tab.loc['pass completion', 'rev']:.0f}%"
```

Fourth quarter, 1:41 left in a one-score game. A receiver dives along the sideline, the ball pinned to his
chest, and tumbles out of bounds. The nearest official, a man in a black cap twenty yards downfield, waves
both arms across his body: incomplete. The home crowd roars at the stadium screen, which is replaying the
catch from a low angle. The losing coach grabs the red flag from his sock, then stops; he isn't allowed to
throw it. Thirty seconds later, with nobody on either sideline having asked, the official in the white cap
walks to the middle of the field, clicks on his microphone and says: *"After review, the ruling on the field
is reversed. The receiver had control of the ball with both feet down in bounds. The pass is complete."* Who
decided that? Why couldn't the coach challenge? And what exactly did "control with both feet down" have to
do with it? This chapter is about the people who run the game and the small set of rules that decide, on
almost every close play, who has the ball.

**You'll be able to…**

- Name the seven officials, find each one on a wide shot, and say which fouls he is most likely to throw a
  flag for.
- Say, for any close play, whether it can be reviewed and by whom: a coach's challenge, a booth review,
  replay assist, or nobody.
- Rule on a catch the way the replay official will (control, feet, then a football act), and say why the
  league rewrote the rule in 2018.
- Apply the rules of the ball: down by contact, forward progress, fumble versus incomplete pass, the fumble
  through the end zone, and backward versus forward passes.
- Call intentional grounding before the flag lands, using the tackle box and the line of scrimmage.
- Decode a referee's announcement and a virtual measurement, and predict "stands", "confirmed" or
  "reversed" before he says it.

## Seven officials, seven jobs

An NFL game is run by seven officials on the field, each wearing a number and, on his back, letters that
name his job (R, U, DJ, LJ, SJ, FJ, BJ). A seven-person crew sounds like a lot until you count what
happens on one snap: 22 players, most of them in contact, spread across 53 yards of width and up to 50 of
depth, in about five seconds. So the crew splits the field and the players into pieces. Each official has a
starting spot, a few players he is responsible for (his *keys*), an area to cover once the ball moves, and a
short list of fouls that are his to call.

::: {#cell-fig-crew .cell execution_count=3}
``` {.python .cell-code}

dfn = defense("4-3_over", "two_high", off)
p = Play(off, dfn, los=40, to_go=10)
fld = p.draw(lateral=(-31.5, 31.5), window=(-16.5, 29.5), title=False)

no_numbers(ax)

CREW = {  # key: (name, (d, w) of the official, (d, w) of his label)
    "R": ("Referee", (-12.0, 5.5), (-14.4, 5.5)),
    "U": ("Umpire", (-11.0, -5.5), (-13.4, -5.5)),
    "DJ": ("Down judge", (0.0, -28.4), (-2.6, -24.0)),
    "LJ": ("Line judge", (0.0, 28.4), (-2.6, 24.0)),
```

Here is what each of them is watching. The table is the short version of the league's own description of
the positions;[^crew] the habits behind it are what let you guess who threw a flag before the referee says.

::: {#tbl-crew .cell tbl-cap='The seven officials: where they start, what they watch, and the calls you\'ll most often see them make.' execution_count=4}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=4}
| Official | Starts | Watches | Typical calls |
|:--|:--|:--|:--|
| **Referee** (R, white cap) | Offensive backfield, 10–12 yards deep, on the quarterback's throwing-arm side | The quarterback and the backs; the snap | Roughing the passer, intentional grounding, fumble or pass by the quarterback; announces every foul and review |
| **Umpire** (U) | Offensive backfield, opposite the referee; on the defensive side for field goals and extra points | The center, guards and the men across from them | Holding (both sides) and false starts inside, illegal hands to the face; spots the ball; checks equipment |
| **Down judge** (DJ) | On the line of scrimmage at one sideline, with the chain crew | The line (who's on it, who moved), the end and receivers on his side, his sideline | Offside, encroachment, false start, illegal formation or motion; forward progress and out of bounds on his side |
| **Line judge** (LJ) | On the line of scrimmage at the other sideline | The same as the down judge, on his side | The same, plus whether a pass was thrown from beyond the line |
| **Side judge** (SJ) | About 20 yards deep near the down judge's sideline | Receivers on his side once they're downfield | Pass interference, illegal contact, catch or no catch, out of bounds |
| **Field judge** (FJ) | About 20 yards deep near the line judge's sideline | Receivers on his side once they're downfield | The same; under one upright on kicks |
| **Back judge** (BJ) | About 25 yards deep in the middle | The tight end and inside receivers, the deep middle, the end line | Deep pass interference, catches in the end zone; under the other upright on kicks |
:::
:::


A few things in that table explain a lot of what you see on Sundays.

**The wing officials own the line of scrimmage.** The [**down judge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-judge) and [**line judge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-line-judge) stand exactly on the line
at the sidelines so they can look straight down it, the only place from which you can see who is offside
and which receivers are on the line (the
[formation rules](../02-personnel-and-formations/02-02-formation-rules-and-vocabulary.qmd) need seven).
Most [pre-snap fouls](../01-foundations/01-05-the-pre-snap-phase.qmd) come from these two. After the snap
they drift downfield and mark where a runner's
[**forward progress**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-forward-progress) stopped: the official you see jog
in and point his foot at the spot.

**The umpire lives in the trenches, and he moved.** For most of football history the [**umpire**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-umpire), the official responsible for the interior line, stood
four or five yards behind the defensive line, in the middle of the linebackers, which is where the holding
happens. It was also where umpires kept getting run over. In 2010 the NFL moved him to the offensive
backfield, opposite the referee, where he watches the same linemen from behind.[^umpire] The trade was
visibility for safety: from behind you see a lineman's hands on a jersey less clearly. (Its side effect was
a slower snap, because the umpire also spots the ball after most plays and now had farther to walk; the
footnote has the brief exceptions the league tried for hurry-up situations.)

**The deep officials are pass officials.** The [**side judge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-side-judge), [**field judge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-field-judge) and [**back judge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-back-judge) are the reason a
deep throw can be judged at all. Each takes a share of the receivers, keeps them between himself and the
sideline or the end line, and rules on
[pass interference and illegal contact](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd), catches and out of bounds.
The seventh official, the side judge, was added in 1978, the same year the league loosened the rules on
pass defense to open up the passing game: more passing meant more eyes downfield.[^seventh]

**Finding them on a wide shot.** The letters are too small to read on most camera angles, so use
geography. Behind the offense there are two officials: the one in the white cap is the referee, the other
is the umpire. On the line at the two sidelines, the one by the chain crew and its sticks is the down
judge, the other the line judge. Of the three deep officials, the one in the middle is the back judge; the
deep wing on the chain crew's side is the side judge, and the one on the far side is the field judge.

**The referee is the boss, and the voice.** The [**referee**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-referee) wears the white cap and leads the crew. His spot,
behind and to the throwing-arm side of the quarterback, lets him watch the one player the rules protect
most: he throws most [roughing-the-passer](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd) flags and decides
whether a quarterback who lost the ball was throwing it or fumbling it. Any official can throw a flag; the
crew gathers, the one who saw the foul tells the referee, and the referee announces it. A flag "picked up"
after that conference usually means another official had a better look.

::: {.callout-note title="Madden vs. real life"}
In a video game a foul is a fact: the code knows a lineman held, and a flag appears. On a real field, a foul
exists only if an official in the right spot sees it. A hold on the far side of a run play can be in no
official's view, and a hold on the play side might be seen by two. That is why "they're letting them play"
is sometimes true, and why the same contact draws a flag in front of the line judge and not behind the
umpire's back. Officiating is a sample, not a census.
:::

### The crew in motion

Starting spots are only half of it. Watch a wide shot of a deep pass and you'll see the crew move as a
unit: the referee stays with the quarterback; the wing officials read the receivers on their side through
the first few yards and then drift downfield, with the line judge usually staying on the line until the
ball is thrown so he can judge whether it was thrown from beyond it; and the deep officials backpedal to
stay deeper and wider than the receivers they're judging, so that every catch is seen from the side or
facing the receiver, never from behind him.

``` {.python .cell-code}
cm.dropback(2.5)
cm.route("X", r.go(20)); cm.route("H", r.seam(18)); cm.route("Y", r.seam(18)); cm.route("Z", r.fade(26))
```

### Who the officials are

NFL officials are mostly part-time, with other careers, working under a labor agreement with their union,
the NFL Referees Association; the league's full-time experiments of 2017, 2019 and 2020 were each dropped. Every official
is graded by the league office on every play, and the grades matter: during the regular season a referee
leads the same crew week after week, but in the playoffs the crews are broken up and rebuilt from the
best-graded individuals at each position, and crew rosters change between seasons as officials retire or
move. In 2026 a contract standoff had the league preparing replacement officials (and a one-year rule
giving New York wider powers to fix their mistakes) until a seven-year deal was agreed in May, so the
regular officials are working this season.[^officials]

Even the referee's microphone has a history: referees were first wired for sound in 1975, under the
league's supervisor of officials Art McNally, who also oversaw the first replay system in 1986 and in 2022
became the first official in the Pro Football Hall of Fame.[^mcnally]

## Replay: three doors into the booth

Officials miss things: they watch a five-second play at full speed from one angle. Replay exists to fix
the misses that matter most without stopping the game every few minutes, through three separate doors,
each with its own rules about who may open it.

**Who is in the booth.** Two groups of people watch the video. In every stadium a **replay official**
(with an assistant) sits in a booth upstairs with the broadcast feeds; he is an official, not a
team employee. In New York, the league's officiating command center (named Art McNally GameDay Central)
watches every game at once. When a review happens, the final decision belongs to the league's senior vice
president of officiating or a designee in New York, consulting the replay official and the referee, who
watches on a field-level monitor (a tablet at the sideline). So: the stadium booth *starts* most reviews, New York *decides* them,
and the referee *announces* them.[^rule15]

Each door was added to fix a problem the last one created:[^replayhist]

- **1986–1991: the first try.** An official in the press box could stop the game to review a play; it was
  slow, overturned little, and was voted out.
- **1999: the challenge flag.** Replay came back with a twist: the *coaches* would decide which plays to
  review, by throwing a red flag, and pay for a failed challenge with a timeout. The booth kept control of
  the final two minutes of each half. The reason: a review stops the clock for a couple of minutes, and a
  *successful* challenge costs nothing, so in a close finish a coach could have used a challenge as a free
  timeout.
- **2011 and 2012: automatic reviews** of every scoring play and every turnover, so a coach no longer had
  to spend a challenge on the biggest calls.
- **2017: New York decides.** The final say moved from the referee, who had watched replays under a
  curtained "hood" on the sideline, to New York, so the same few people judge every review.
- **2019: pass interference, for one season** (the story is in
  [Contact Rules and Penalties](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd)). Almost nothing was overturned.
- **2021: replay assist.** The booth began fixing clear-cut objective facts on its own, without a formal
  stop, and its powers grew in 2024, 2025 and 2026 (below).

Every review uses the same standard: the ruling on the field is changed only on **clear and obvious**
visual evidence. That produces the three outcomes in every announcement. *Reversed* means the video shows
the call was wrong. *Confirmed* means the video shows it was right. *Stands* means the video doesn't show
enough either way, so the call on the field survives. For the game, "confirmed" and "stands" are the same:
the play counts as called, and a coach who challenged loses his timeout either way. The difference is what
the video showed, and that is what you can predict: when the camera can't see the key moment (a ball at the
bottom of a pile, a knee hidden by a body), the answer is almost always "stands".

### Door 1: the coach's challenge

A [**coach's challenge**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-coach-s-challenge) is the head coach asking for a
review by throwing a red flag onto the field before the next snap. The rules make it scarce on purpose:[^challenges]

- Each team gets **two challenges** a game. Since 2024 it gets **a third if either of the first two
  succeeds**; before that, both had to succeed.
- A team must have a **timeout** left to challenge, and it **loses that timeout if the challenge fails**.
- A coach may not challenge after the **two-minute warning** of either half, in **overtime**, or any play
  the booth reviews automatically (a score, a turnover). A coach who throws his flag anyway is charged a
  timeout, or 15 yards if he has none left, but the booth still reviews the play if it would have anyway.
- Only certain rulings are reviewable: whether a pass was caught, whether a runner was down, in bounds or
  across the goal line, the spot relative to the line to gain or the goal line, who recovered a loose ball,
  too many men on the field. Judgment fouls, holding or interference, are not. A flag elsewhere on the play
  doesn't block a challenge: a coach can challenge a catch on a play that also had a holding call, and the
  foul is enforced (or declined) after the ruling is settled.

That third rule has a story. On Thanksgiving 2012, Houston's Justin Forsett was clearly touched down early
in what became an 81-yard touchdown run against Detroit. Lions coach Jim Schwartz, furious, threw his red
flag, even though every touchdown was already reviewed by the booth. Under the rule of the time, an illegal
challenge drew a 15-yard penalty *and cancelled the automatic review*, so the touchdown stood unreviewed,
and Houston won 34–31 in overtime. The next spring the league changed the penalty to a charged timeout and
kept the review.[^schwartz]

Why make challenges expensive? Because a free challenge would be thrown on every close play, and each
review costs two or three minutes. The timeout charge turns a challenge into a bet (the chance of winning
times what the reversal is worth, against the chance of losing times what a timeout is worth later), which
the [game-management staff](../01-foundations/01-04-what-a-play-really-is.qmd) upstairs must make in the
few seconds before the next snap. It's also why an offense that likes the call hurries to the line: once
the ball is snapped, the play can't be challenged
([In-Game Adjustments and Tempo](../08-the-chess-match/08-04-in-game-adjustments-and-tempo.qmd)).

And it's why challenges are rarer than you'd guess. In 2025 coaches threw 151 challenges in
272 regular-season games, about 0\.28 per team per game, and won
52% of them; over 2016–2025 the success rate was 46%.[^reviewcalc]
A coach who is right about half the time, and is only betting on plays he's fairly sure of, is telling you
how hard it is to see a play clearly from the sideline in ten seconds.

### Door 2: booth review

A [**booth review**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-booth-review) is started by the replay official in the
stadium (or by New York), not by a coach. It covers:

- **every scoring play** (touchdowns, field goals, safeties) and **every try**;
- **every turnover** as ruled on the field (an interception, a fumble recovered by the defense or knocked
  through its end zone, a muffed kick recovered by the kicking team), and every ruling that the offense came
  up **short on fourth down**;
- **every reviewable play after the two-minute warning of each half and in overtime**.

Most booth reviews never stop the game: a touchdown is looked at during the celebration, and if the video
agrees, the game goes on. If the booth wants a closer look, it buzzes the referee and the game stops. A
[**replay review**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-replay-review) of either kind ends the same way, with
the referee at the middle of the field reading New York's decision.

A reversal also fixes the clock. The clock is reset to the moment the ball should have been dead and then
runs or stops as the correct ruling dictates: an incompletion reversed to a catch in bounds puts the ball
where the play should have ended, with the clock running as it would have. After the two-minute warning, a reversal
that turns a stopped clock into a running one also brings a **10-second runoff**, which either team can
avoid only by spending a timeout. Those runoffs, and the end-of-half arithmetic around them, belong to
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).[^clockreview]

### Door 3: replay assist

The newest door is the quietest. [**Replay assist**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-replay-assist) lets the
booth tell the crew about a clear-cut objective fact before the next snap, usually with no stoppage you'd
notice: the ball was spotted a yard short of the line to gain, the runner's knee was down before the ball
came out, the receiver's second foot landed out of bounds, two seconds should go back on the clock. It began
in 2021 as a way to fix the obvious without a coach gambling a timeout on it.

If the booth can fix a wrong spot for free, why would a coach ever challenge one? Because replay assist acts
only when the answer is *clear at once*, in the few seconds before the next snap. If the booth stays quiet,
a coach who thinks a longer look would change the call still has his red flag; the rules say replay assist
never takes that away.

Since 2024 it has had a little power over flags, always limited to the objective piece of a foul. In 2024 it
could wipe out a roughing-the-passer flag for a hit to the head when the video showed no contact with the
head or neck, a grounding flag when the passer was clearly outside the pocket, and a late-hit flag when the
runner was clearly still in bounds; the judgment part of roughing (was the hit late?) is still not
reviewable. In 2025 it added five more: a hit to a defenseless player's head or neck, a face mask, a
horse-collar tackle, tripping, and roughing or running into the kicker, each only when the video plainly
shows the key contact never happened. It **cannot add** a foul that nobody called. And in 2026 its staff
may **consult** with the crew on ejections for flagrant acts: *football* acts (a hit during the play so
violent it warrants ejection, such as a launch into a defenseless receiver's head) and *non-football* acts
(a punch away from the play). Some reports describe that as replay ejecting players; the league's official
wording is only that it may consult.[^assist]

What the NFL still doesn't have is a **sky judge**: an official in the booth with the power to call or wipe
out any foul in real time. Spring leagues have used one (the USFL's sky judge wiped out a wrong face-mask
flag in a 2023 playoff game), and the idea has been proposed in the NFL since at least 2019.[^skyjudge] The
objections are practical: it would slow the game, and it would make every play (on which, coaches like to
say, somebody is holding) a candidate for a flag. So the league has expanded replay one narrow, objective
slice at a time.

Two patterns are worth carrying into a game. Catch-or-no-catch rulings make up about

catch. And rulings of a *catch* are reviewed more than twice as often as rulings of *incomplete* (overturned

## The catch

Nothing in the rulebook has caused more arguments than the definition of a catch, because of the stakes.
If it was a catch and the ball then comes loose, it's a **fumble**: a live ball anyone can recover. If it
wasn't, it's an **incomplete pass**: dead, and the offense keeps it. So the rule has to separate
*possessing* a ball from merely *touching* it, at full speed, often while someone is hitting the receiver.

Today's rule, rewritten in 2018, says a player has made a
[**catch**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-catch-completed-pass) when, in bounds, he does three things in
order:[^catchrule]

1. **Control.** He secures control of the ball in his hands or arms before it touches the ground.
2. **Feet (or a body part) down.** He touches the ground in bounds with both feet, or with any part of his
   body other than his hands (a knee, a hip, an elbow).
3. **Time.** After the first two, he makes an *act common to the game*: tucks the ball away, turns upfield,
   takes an extra step, reaches the ball toward the line, wards off a defender. Or he keeps control long
   enough that he *could* have.

Three clarifications do most of the work on replays.

- **Slight movement isn't a loss of control**, and a bobble he then secures is fine, as long as the ball never
  touches the ground in between.
- **The ground matters only before gate 3.** If he finishes gate 3 on his feet (a third step, a turn, a
  reach) and *then* falls and the ball comes out, it was a catch and then a fumble, or simply a catch if he
  was down by contact. But if he is falling *while* he catches it, so that he hits the ground before he has
  had time for any football act, the ground is part of the catch: he must keep control when he lands. If
  the ball pops loose and touches the ground then, the pass is incomplete.
- **A tie goes to the offense.** If an offensive and a defensive player catch the ball at the same moment and
  both keep it, it's the offense's ball. If one had it first and the other wrestled in, it belongs to the
  first.

An interception is judged by exactly the same three gates.

### Why the rule was rewritten

For most of the 2010s the rule had an extra clause that produced some of the most hated rulings in league
history. A receiver who went to the ground "in the process of the catch" had to keep control of the ball
*after* hitting the ground, the so-called *survive the ground* requirement, no matter how many steps he had
taken or how obviously he had possessed it. The clause was meant to make the rule objective: instead of
asking officials to judge whether a player had possession long enough, it gave them a test they could see on
video. The trouble was that the objective test kept ruling against what everyone watching had seen. Three
plays made it untenable:[^catchhist]

- **Calvin Johnson, Lions at Bears, September 12, 2010.** Trailing 19–14 with 31 seconds left, Johnson
  caught a pass in the end zone, landed with both feet and his backside, and put the ball down on the turf
  as he rolled to get up. Ruled incomplete; the booth upheld it. The Lions lost by five, and "the Calvin
  Johnson rule" entered the vocabulary.
- **Dez Bryant, Cowboys at Packers, divisional playoffs, January 11, 2015.** On fourth-and-2 late in the
  game, Bryant caught a deep ball, took three steps as he fell, reached for the goal line, and the ball
  moved when it hit the turf at the 1. Ruled a catch, reversed on Green Bay's challenge; the Packers won
  (the Film room below walks through it).
- **Jesse James, Patriots at Steelers, December 17, 2017.** With 34 seconds left and Pittsburgh down
  27–24, James caught a short pass a few yards from the goal line, went to a knee *untouched* (so he wasn't down: in the NFL
  a runner needs contact, as the next section explains), and lunged across the goal line; the ball moved
  as it hit the turf. Ruled a touchdown, reversed by the booth. The Steelers lost the game and, as it
  turned out, home-field advantage in the playoffs.

The owners approved a rewrite 32–0 in March 2018. Here is precisely what changed. Under the old rule, a
receiver who went to the ground "in the process of the catch" had to survive the ground *however many steps
or reaches he had made on the way down*: falling cancelled them. Under the new rule, a football act made
before the ball comes loose (a third step, a reach for the line, or time enough to make one) finishes the
catch, even if he is falling, and only a receiver who hits the ground *before* he has made one must still
survive it. (The 2018 announcement said "football move"; the rulebook says "act common to the game".) The
league's football chiefs said publicly that Bryant's and James's catches would now count.[^catchnew]

Would Calvin Johnson's? Try it with the gates. Control: yes, high in the end zone. Feet: both feet, then
his backside. Time: the argument. He went to the ground as he caught it, so he must keep control through
the landing unless he had time for a football act first. If you see him land, hold the ball, and only then
use it to push himself up, he had the time, and it's a touchdown today. If you see one continuous fall
with the ball coming loose as part of it, it's still incomplete. The league never ruled on it publicly,
and that is the honest answer: it's a judgment about time.

Name the trade: the old rule was objective and produced absurd results; the new one matches what people
see, at the price of a judgment ("was that lunge a football act or part of the fall?") at its center.

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The ball touched the ground, so it's incomplete." The ball is allowed to touch the ground during a catch,
as long as the receiver keeps control of it, with his hands under it or the ball pinned to his body. What it
can't do is help him: a ball trapped against the turf with no hand under it, or one that pops loose when he
lands before he has had time for a football act, is incomplete.
:::

### Sidelines and end zones

Two places put extra weight on gate 2. At the **sideline**, a receiver needs both feet (or another body
part) down in bounds with control; one foot, as in college football, isn't enough. Since 2008 there has been
no "force-out" ruling either: a receiver pushed out of bounds in the air before getting both feet down has
not caught the ball, however sure the official is that he would have landed in bounds (unless he had control
and was held up and *carried* out).[^forceout] And because a toe-tap leaves no time for a football act, he
must keep control as he falls out; a ball jarred loose when he hits the ground out of bounds is incomplete.

In the **end zone**, the catch is the touchdown, so the receiver must complete all three gates there; a
runner who already has the ball only needs it to touch the plane of the goal line (the
[end zone](../01-foundations/01-01-the-game-in-fifteen-minutes.qmd) is generous that way). A receiver who
completes the catch short of the line and then reaches across has scored, which is how Jesse James's play
would be ruled today.

## Down, progress and the whistle

Most plays end with a ball carrier going down, and the NFL's definition differs from college's. A runner is
[**down by contact**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-down-by-contact) when any part of his body other than
his hands or feet touches the ground *and he has been touched by an opponent*. The order of those two can
go either way. If nobody touched him, he isn't down: a running back who slips on wet turf, or a returner who
kneels to field a bouncing kick, may get up and keep running. But if a defender touches him *while* he is
on the ground, he is down right there, which is why defenders are coached to "touch him down" rather than
assume the play is over. In college football the runner is down as soon as his knee touches, contact or
not.[^downrule] (A runner who slides feet-first or simply gives himself up is down where he does it; that's
how quarterbacks protect themselves.)

The order of events matters more than anything else on these plays. If the ball comes out *before* the knee
(or elbow, or hip) touches after contact, it's a fumble: live, and anyone's. If the knee touches first, the
runner was down and the ball coming out afterward doesn't matter. On television these are separated by a
few frames of video, which is why they're among the most-reviewed rulings in the data above.

**Forward progress** decides *where* the play ended. You met it in
[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd): the
ball is spotted at the farthest point it reached toward the goal line before the runner was stopped, not
where he ended up after a pile drove him back. The same idea tells officials when to blow the whistle. A
runner wrapped up and held upright, his legs still churning, has had his forward progress stopped even
though he hasn't gone down, and the officials will whistle the play dead rather than let a pile of
defenders keep shoving him backward (or strip the ball from a man who has stopped moving forward). It also
protects runners at the goal line: a back who gets the ball across the plane and is knocked back has scored.
(Only being *driven* back counts: a quarterback who retreats on his own and is sacked is spotted where he
goes down.) And it affects the clock: a runner stopped in bounds and then shoved out of bounds was down *in bounds*, so the
clock keeps running, a detail that matters in [the two-minute drill](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd).

### The whistle, and the 2008 lesson

The whistle is the one tool officials can't take back. Once it blows, the play is dead, whatever happens
next. (When one is blown by mistake with the ball still live, the team with the ball can usually take it
where the whistle killed the play or replay the down; a pass in the air is simply replayed.)[^whistle] That
used to put replay in an impossible position: if an official ruled a play over and the video showed a
fumble, replay could fix the ruling but couldn't know who would have recovered the ball.

The play that made everyone face this came on September 14, 2008. Denver trailed San Diego 38–31 with 1:17
left, second-and-goal at the 1. Jay Cutler dropped back, and the ball slipped out of his hand as he started
to throw; a Charger fell on it. Referee Ed Hochuli ruled it an incomplete pass and blew his whistle. Replay
showed a fumble, but because the whistle had already killed the play, the Chargers couldn't be given the
ball. Denver kept it at the 10, where Cutler had lost it, scored on fourth-and-goal with 29 seconds left,
went for two, and won 39–38.[^hochuli]
Hochuli, one of the most respected referees of his era, publicly apologized.

Two things changed. In 2009 the owners passed what was quickly nicknamed the "Hochuli rule": replay may now
award the ball to the team that recovered it when the recovery is clear and in the *immediate continuing
action*, even after a whistle.[^hochulirule] And the officials' habit changed:
on a bang-bang fumble, they are taught to hold the whistle, let the players finish the scramble for the
ball, and rule a fumble when in doubt, because replay can turn a fumble back into a dead ball cleanly but
can't recreate a recovery that never happened. That is why you now see a defender scoop up a loose ball and
run the other way while everyone else has stopped.

## Pass or fumble: the quarterback's arm

A close cousin of down-or-fumble is pass-or-fumble, and it comes up every time a pass rusher hits a
quarterback as he throws. The rule is about the arm. Once the quarterback, holding the ball, starts his arm
moving forward to throw, anything that comes out is a forward pass, and if it hits the ground it's
incomplete. If he loses the ball *before* his arm starts forward, or while he is pulling it back down
to tuck it after deciding not to throw, it's a fumble.

The second half of that sentence was not always true. Until 2013 the rulebook had the **tuck rule**: if the
quarterback started forward and then brought the ball back toward his body, it was still a pass until he
had tucked it all the way in. It is remembered for the snowy January 2002 playoff in Foxborough, when Tom
Brady lost the ball under Charles Woodson's hit, the Raiders recovered, and replay called it an incomplete
pass; New England kept the ball and won in overtime. The league abolished the rule in 2013.[^tuck] Today
the same play is a fumble.

Who reviews it depends on the call on the field. When the field rules a fumble that the defense recovered,
it's a turnover, so the booth reviews it automatically. When the field rules an incomplete pass, there's no
turnover to trigger the booth, so before the two-minute warning the defense's coach usually has to throw his
red flag (unless replay assist steps in on the possession), which is the moment you see a coach grab it
on a strip-sack ruled incomplete. Either way, watch
the arm, not the ball: if the arm was coming forward with the ball in the hand, it's a pass.

## A fumble through the end zone

Now the harshest rule in the book. When a fumble goes out of bounds, the general rule is generous to the
team that fumbled: it keeps the ball. If the ball went out going backward, it's spotted where it went out;
if it went out going *forward*, it comes back to the spot of the fumble, so that nobody gains yards by
fumbling forward on purpose.

The exception is the opponent's end zone. A
[**fumble through the end zone**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-fumble-through-the-end-zone-touchback),
a ball fumbled forward into the end zone that goes out of bounds there, out the side or out the back, is a
**touchback**: the defense gets the ball at its own 20, even though no defender ever touched it.[^fumbleoob]
A fumble that stays *in* the end zone is simpler: if the offense falls on it there, it's a touchdown (on fourth
down or late in a half, only the man who fumbled may, as the box below explains); if the defense does, it's a touchback. And the mirror image works against the offense in its own end zone: a
ball it fumbles there that goes out of bounds (or one it fumbles in the field that it sends back into its
own end zone and out) is a **safety**, because the offense supplied the push that put the ball there.

::: {#cell-fig-fumble-oob .cell execution_count=10}

Why would the rules punish the offense so hard? The logic is about territory, not possession. The end zone
belongs to the defending team, and when a ball goes dead there because of something the other team did (a
punt rolls through, a kickoff sails out the back), it's a touchback, like the
[touchbacks on punts](09-01-kicking-and-punting.qmd). A fumble into your end zone and out is treated the
same way. The rule is consistent; it just doesn't feel fair, because the defense did nothing to earn it. It is one of the most criticized rules in the book; the competition committee looked at
softening it in 2017 and again in February 2024 and kept it both times, arguing that the ball carrier is
responsible for the ball and that nobody had a workable alternative. It is unchanged in the 2026
rulebook.[^fumblecomm]

The rule shapes technique: it's why a ball carrier stretching for the pylon is taking a real gamble, and
why defenders near the goal line punch at the ball instead of wrapping up.

::: {.callout-important title="Why it exists: the fourth-down fumble rule"}
On September 10, 1978, with the Raiders trailing the Chargers in the final seconds, Ken Stabler, about to
be sacked, fumbled the ball forward; teammates batted and kicked it toward the goal line, and Dave Casper
fell on it in the end zone for the winning touchdown. The "Holy
Roller" was legal then. The next season the league made it impossible: on fourth down, and on any down after
the two-minute warning, only the player who fumbled may recover and advance the ball. If a teammate
recovers it, the ball comes back to the spot of the fumble (or the spot of recovery, if that is behind
it).[^holyroller] The rule exists to stop an offense from fumbling forward on purpose when it has nothing
left to lose.
:::

## Backward passes and forward passes

Football allows exactly **one forward pass per play**, and it must be thrown from behind the line of
scrimmage. It allows any number of [**backward passes**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-backward-pass)
(also called [**laterals**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-lateral)), from anywhere, by anyone, at any
time. The two are treated very differently when they hit the ground:

- A **forward pass** that hits the ground is **incomplete**. The ball is dead, and the offense keeps it.
- A **backward pass** that hits the ground is **still live**, exactly like a fumble. Either team may recover
  it, and either team may advance it.

Which is which? The test is the ball's direction: compare the yard line where it left the passer's hand
with the yard line where it is first touched (or first hits the ground). If the second is closer to the
opponent's goal, the pass was forward. If it's the same yard line or behind, the pass was backward, so a
pass thrown perfectly parallel to the line counts as **backward**.[^lateral] Notice that it's the ball's
path that counts, not the players' positions on the field. (This chapter calls the yard line where the ball
leaves the passer's hand the *release line*; that's our label for the diagrams, not a rulebook term.)

The forward pass's two limits are fouls of their own, and the line judge watches for the first. A forward
pass is **illegal** if the passer's *entire body* and the ball are beyond the line of scrimmage when he lets
go, which is the call you see on a quarterback who scrambles up to the line and flips it at the last
moment: one foot still behind the line keeps it legal. A **second forward pass** on the same play is illegal
too. Either costs a loss of down and 5 yards.

Why does a dropped backward pass stay live? Because the rules treat it as the normal case. A backward pass
is just a handoff through the air: the ball stays a runner's ball, and if he doesn't catch it, it's loose,
like any fumble. The *forward* pass is the special case, the one the rules ration (one per play, from
behind the line) and give a special ending: when it fails, the play stops and the offense keeps the ball,
paying with the down. The result shows up in three places on a broadcast:

- **Pitches and option plays.** A pitch on the
  [option](../03-the-run-game/03-04-option-football.qmd) is a backward pass. Drop it and you've fumbled, in
  effect, which is why option teams drill the pitch relentlessly.
- **Screens.** Most shotgun screens are forward passes, caught closer to the line than the five or six
  yards deep where the quarterback let go. But a bubble or swing screen to a player who has drifted back
  level with the quarterback may be backward, so defenders are coached to scoop up every dropped screen and
  run: if it was backward, the ball is theirs. (The
  [illegal-man-downfield rule](../04-the-passing-game/04-06-rpos.qmd) applies only to a forward pass thrown
  beyond the line, so on a true backward pass linemen may already be blocking downfield.)
- **Last-play desperation.** The multi-lateral kickoff return or final snap, the ball pitched backward
  again and again, is legal because every pitch is backward.

The most famous backward pass in NFL history came in a wild-card game on January 8, 2000, on a kickoff
with 16 seconds left: Tennessee's Frank Wycheck threw the ball across the field to Kevin Dyson, who ran 75
yards for the winning touchdown. Replay couldn't show that the throw had gone forward, so the ruling of a
legal lateral stood, and the "Music City Miracle" became the standard illustration of the rule.[^musiccity]

## Intentional grounding and the tackle box

[Quarterback Play](../04-the-passing-game/04-07-quarterback-play.qmd) introduced the
[throwaway](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-throwaway) and the rule that limits it. Here is the full rule,
and the reasoning behind it.

[**Intentional grounding**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-intentional-grounding) is a foul when a passer
who is facing an imminent loss of yardage because of the rush throws a pass that isn't in the direction and
vicinity of an eligible receiver. (The rulebook says *originally* eligible: eligible when the ball was
snapped, so a lineman who has wandered downfield doesn't count as a target.) Three conditions, all
needed:[^grounding]

1. **Pressure.** He must be facing a likely sack. A quarterback under no pressure who throws the ball into
   the turf has wasted a down, but he hasn't grounded it.
2. **No realistic target.** The pass isn't thrown near an eligible receiver. "Near" is a judgment, and
   throwing the ball well over the head of a covered receiver in the right part of the field counts.
3. **Inside the tackle box.** The [**tackle box**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-tackle-box), which the
   rulebook calls the *pocket area*, is the region between the outside edges of where the two offensive
   tackles lined up, running from the line of scrimmage all the way back to the offense's own end line.
   It's fixed by where the *tackles* aligned at the snap: a tight end lined up outside a tackle doesn't
   widen it, and it doesn't move when the quarterback does.

The exception is what makes the box matter: **a passer who is or has been outside the tackle box may throw
the ball away freely, as long as it lands at or beyond the line of scrimmage** (extended to the sidelines),
including out of bounds past it. Since the 2024 rulebook he counts as outside the box if any part of his
body, or the ball, is outside it. And "has been" means what it says: a quarterback who escapes the box and
then drifts back inside it keeps the exception for the rest of the play.

The penalty is built to cost about what the sack would have: **loss of down and 10 yards** from the previous
spot, or loss of down at the spot of the pass if that is farther back, and **a safety** if he throws it
from his own end zone. The other exception is the **spike**: a quarterback who throws the ball straight
into the ground immediately after the snap, to stop the clock, loses only the down (more in
[The Clock, the Two-Minute Drill, and Fourth Down](../10-situational-football/10-04-clock-and-game-management.qmd)).

Why draw the line at the box? A sack is something the defense earned. If a quarterback could always throw
the ball into the ground to avoid one, the pass rush would lose much of its value, so inside the pocket,
where the defense has him trapped, he must at least throw toward someone. A quarterback who has escaped the
pocket has beaten the rush himself; letting him throw it away (provided it reaches the line, so he can't
just dump it at his feet) rewards the escape. The 2024 wording tilted that balance a little further his way.

The best-known grounding call of recent decades shows the safety clause at work: on New England's first
offensive play of Super Bowl XLVI, February 5, 2012, Tom Brady, pressured in his own end zone, threw deep down
the middle to nobody. Grounding from the end zone is a safety, and the Giants led 2–0 before the Patriots had
gained a yard. They won by four.[^xlvi]

The "has been outside" clause is the subtle part, and it's easiest to see in motion.

``` {.python .cell-code}
sp.path("WDE", [(-3.5, -4.5), (-7.0, -1.2), (-8.8, 0.6)], absolute=True, speed=5.5)   # flushes him, overruns
```

## The measurement: chains, cameras, and the spot

[Downs, Distance, and Field Position](../01-foundations/01-02-downs-distance-and-field-position.qmd)
described the chain crew's ritual: two sticks joined by ten yards of chain, carried onto the field to see
whether the ball's nose had reached the front stick. Since 2025 that walk is mostly gone. A [**virtual measurement**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-virtual-measurement), often
called a [**Hawk-Eye measurement**](../../appendices/glossary.qmd#gl-hawk-eye-measurement) after the Sony
system that does it, uses six 8K cameras around the stadium to measure the distance from where the ball sits
to the line to gain, and hands the answer to the officials in about 30 seconds, while a virtual graphic of
the measurement plays on the broadcast and the stadium screens. The chain crew stays on the sideline as the
visible marker for players and coaches, and as a backup if the cameras fail.[^hawkeye]

At the start of the series an official clipped the chain at the nearest 5-yard stripe; laying that clip back on the same stripe puts the rear stick exactly where the series began, so the front stick, ten yards on, can be compared with the nose of the ball (the ball is drawn larger than scale). But in both, the ball sits where an official spotted it by eye (the shaded band is an illustrative margin of error, not a measured one): the cameras measure from that spot; they don't choose it.](09-04-officiating-replay-and-rules-of-the-ball_files/figure-html/fig-measure-output-1.svg){#fig-measure}
:::
:::


The change is a nice lesson in two words that sound alike. *Precision* is how finely you can measure;
*accuracy* is whether you measured from the right place. The chains were not very precise (a clip laid by
hand, a chain pulled taut by eye), and they were slow. The cameras are extremely precise. But they measure
from the spot, and the spot is still a human judgment: an official running alongside the play, often
looking through a pile of bodies, deciding where the ball's nose was when forward progress stopped. A
measurement precise to a fraction of an inch, taken from a spot that could be off by a foot, is only as
accurate as the spot. That is why the spot itself can still be reviewed, but only in narrow cases: on a
play that's challenged or booth-reviewed, or through replay assist, the booth can move the spot when the
video clearly shows where the ball was relative to the line to gain or the goal line. (Who decides to
measure at all? The referee. A team's captain can ask him for one, but it's his call.)[^measure]

::: {.callout-caution title="Common misconception"}
"The cameras decide first downs now." They decide the *measurement*. The officials still spot the ball by
eye, and the yellow line on your screen is still the broadcaster's drawing, not an official mark. When a
spot looks wrong, the cameras can't help; only the replay booth's look at the spot can.
:::

## Reading the referee's announcement

Every announcement follows the same grammar, and once you know it you can usually finish the referee's
sentence for him. For a foul, the order is: **what** the foul was, **who** committed it (offense or defense,
and the player's number), **how much** it costs and **from where**, and **what happens to the down**.
For a review it's: the **outcome** (stands, confirmed, reversed), the **reason** in a sentence, and the
**result** (the new down, distance and spot, and anything about the clock).

::: {#tbl-announce .cell tbl-cap='Six announcements decoded. The words in quotation marks are the typical form; referees vary the wording a little.' execution_count=15}

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display .cell-output-markdown execution_count=15}
| What the referee says | What it means |
|:--|:--|
| “Holding, number 72, offense. Ten-yard penalty. Repeat second down.” | An accepted offensive holding foul: 10 yards from the previous spot, and the down is played again. |
| “Pass interference, defense, number 24. Spot foul. Automatic first down.” | Defensive pass interference: the ball goes to the spot of the foul with a new set of downs. |
| “Offsetting fouls. Repeat third down.” | A foul by each team; they cancel and the down is replayed. |
| “Illegal formation, offense. The penalty is declined. Fourth down.” | The defense chose the play's result over the yards (a third-down incompletion, say). |
| “After review, the ruling on the field stands. Third down.” | The video wasn't clear enough to overturn the call, whichever way it was. |
| “After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The runner's knee was down before the ball came out. There is no fumble. Second down.” | The booth turned a turnover back into a tackle: the down-by-contact order of events. |
:::
:::


The enforcement words (*spot foul*, *declined*, *automatic first down*) are taught in
[Contact Rules and Penalties](09-03-contact-rules-and-penalties.qmd). Before the announcement, the referee's arm signal tells you most of it, and a
few signals cover most flags: a hand gripping the other wrist for holding; both hands on the hips for
offside or encroachment; forearms rolling over each other in front of the chest for a false start; both
open hands pushed forward from the shoulders for pass interference; one wrist chopping the other above the
head for a personal foul; and both arms, held parallel, waved diagonally across the body for intentional
grounding.[^signals]

In 2025 an average game had 12\.8 accepted penalties, and the crews' averages ran from
10\.2 (Brad Allen's crew) to 14\.6
(Adrian Hill's).[^crewcalc] That spread sounds large until you set it against the noise. A
single game's total varies a lot (the standard deviation was about 4\.3 penalties), so a
crew's 16- or 17-game average would wander about ±2\.2 around the league average by luck
alone. Most crews sit inside that band. And the ranking usually doesn't hold: the correlation between a
crew's 2024 and 2025 averages was 0\.28, and across the ten seasons from 2016 to 2025 the
year-to-year correlation was usually weak (median 0\.28), occasionally strong (it ranged
from \-0\.35 to 0\.76). Only 12 of the 16 crews landed in the same
half of the table both years.

So crews differ a little, and inconsistently. Teams are hardly more predictable: a team's own rate of
accepted fouls has a median year-to-year correlation of 0\.32 over the same seasons.
Most of a single game's flag count, in other words, is noise: who happened to hold on which snap, in front
of which official. And some of the variation is the league's doing, not the crews': the league-wide average swings with points of
emphasis, from 11\.2 to 13\.5 per game across 2016–2025, which is why a
preseason memo telling officials to watch for a particular foul can move the numbers for every crew at once.

## Film room

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Cowboys at Packers, 2014 divisional playoffs, the catch that wasn't"}
Find the play: January 11, 2015, fourth quarter, 4:42 left, fourth-and-2 at the Green Bay 32, Dallas down
26–21. Watch Dez Bryant and count the gates. Control: yes, above the cornerback. Feet: yes. Time: the
argument. He takes three steps while falling and stretches the ball toward the goal line, and the ball
hits the turf and moves as he lands. Under the 2014 rule, he was going to the ground in the process of the catch, so his three
steps and his reach didn't count; he had to keep control through the ground, and replay ruled he hadn't.
Under the 2018 rule, those steps and that reach are acts common to the game, made before the ball touched
down, so the catch was complete before he landed. Watch the replay twice, once with each
rule in your head, and you'll understand why the league changed it.
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: Patriots at Jets, 2017, the touchback nobody recovered"}
October 15, 2017, fourth quarter, 8:31 left, the Jets down 24–14 at the New England 4. Austin
Seferian-Jenkins catches a short pass and turns toward the goal line; as he dives for it, with a defender
on him, the ball comes loose. Ruled a touchdown, it went to the booth as a scoring play. Replay ruled he lost the
ball before crossing the line and didn't regain control until he was out of bounds in the end zone: a
fumble out of the end zone. That second point was the argument afterward; two former league officiating
chiefs said they wouldn't have overturned it, and the league stood by the call. No defender recovered
anything, and the Patriots got the ball at their own 20. New England won by seven.[^asj]
:::

::: {.callout-note title="Film room: the 2025 season, the cameras arrive"}
Pick any 2025 or 2026 game and wait for a close spot on third or fourth down. Watch the order of events: the
official spots the ball by eye, the referee signals for a measurement, and within about half a minute the
stadium screen shows the virtual line against the ball's nose. The chain crew never leaves the sideline. Then
watch the reactions: players and coaches now argue about the spot, the only human part left, and almost
never about the measurement.
:::

## Watch for it on Sunday

::: {.callout-tip title="Watch for it: the ref's mic"}
Every time a flag flies, or a ruling is close, make two calls before the referee turns on his microphone:

1. **Name the official.** Who threw it? A flag from the line of scrimmage at a sideline is the down or line
   judge (pre-snap foul, likely false start, offside or illegal formation). A flag from deep downfield is a
   side, field or back judge (likely pass interference or illegal contact). A flag from the backfield, near
   the quarterback, is the referee (roughing the passer, grounding) or the umpire (holding in the middle).
2. **Name the foul or the ruling**, and its result: how many yards, from where, and the down that follows.
3. **On every review, predict the outcome**: *reversed*, *confirmed* or *stands*. First ask who started it
   (a coach's flag, or the booth: after the two-minute warning, a score, a turnover). Then ask which angle would settle
   it. If the decisive moment is hidden (a pile, a body in the way), say *stands*.
4. **On every close catch, count the gates out loud**: control, feet, time.

Keep a tally for one game, and add your review predictions to your prediction log. You'll miss plenty at
first; by the end of a season the official-then-foul habit will have you announcing it before the referee
does.
:::

**Which official made the call? Can the coach challenge? Who decides, and what will the referee announce?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The field judge**, the deep wing on the far side from the chain crew. **The coach can't challenge**:
it's after the two-minute warning, so only the booth can review it (his flag would just cost a timeout).
The replay official starts the review, New York decides, the referee announces.

The review runs the gates. **Control** and **feet**: yes, both feet in bounds with the ball secured.
**Time**: a toe-tap leaves no time for a football act, so he had to **keep control through his landing out
of bounds**, and he did: a ball that shifts while his hands stay on it is *slight movement*, and it never
touched the ground. So: **"After review, the ruling on the field is reversed. The pass is complete,"** dead
where he went out. No 10-second runoff: a catch that ends out of bounds stops the clock anyway. (Had the
ball come loose and hit the ground, it would "stand" or be "confirmed": incomplete.)
:::
:::

**What's the ruling, and who gets the ball where? What if the ball had gone out of bounds at the 1 instead?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**A fumble through the end zone: touchback**, the defense's ball at its own 20, though it never recovered
anything. As a turnover, the booth reviews it automatically, asking in order: **did the ball break the
plane, or touch the pylon, while he still had it?** (touchdown); was he touched and down before it came
out? (fourth-and-goal at the 1); did the loose ball really go out in the end zone? (A loose ball that hits
the pylon is out there too: touchback.)

Out of bounds *at the 1* instead, the offense keeps it, back at the spot of the fumble: fourth-and-goal from
the 1. A few feet of turf, worth several
[expected points](../13-analytics-and-data/13-02-expected-points-and-success-rate.qmd): that's why coaches
tell runners to carry the ball high and tight near the goal line.

**Who threw the flag, and for what? Where is the ball, and what down is it?**

::: {.callout-tip title="Answer" collapse="true"}
**The referee, for intentional grounding**: he watches the quarterback, and grounding is his call.
*Pressure*: the end was closing. *No receiver near*: nobody. *The box*: he was outside it, so the exception
applies, **but only if the ball reaches the line of scrimmage**, and this one landed a yard short. (A yard
past the line, it would have been a legal throwaway.)

The penalty is **loss of down and 10 yards** from the previous spot (the spot of the pass, about 7 yards
back, isn't farther), so the ball goes back to the 20 and it's **fourth-and-18**: almost certainly a punt.
*"Intentional grounding, offense. Ten-yard penalty and loss of down. Fourth down."* Replay assist can't save
him: being outside the pocket isn't what made this one grounding.
:::
:::

## Takeaways

- **Seven officials split the field and the players**: the referee (white cap) the quarterback, the umpire
  the interior line, the down and line judges the line of scrimmage and sidelines, the side, field and back
  judges the receivers downfield. Where a flag came from tells you what it is likely to be.
- **Replay asks two questions in order.** Is the ruling reviewable at all (judgment fouls aren't)? Does the
  booth review it automatically (scores, tries, turnovers, short on fourth down, after the two-minute
  warning, overtime)? If not, only a coach's challenge, paid for with a timeout, can open it. Replay assist
  runs alongside on clear objective facts and the objective part of a short list of flags. There is no sky
  judge.
- **Reversals need clear and obvious evidence**, so a hidden moment usually "stands"; "stands" and
  "confirmed" leave the play exactly as called.
- **A catch is three gates: control, feet down, then time.** Since 2018 a football act made on the way down
  finishes the catch; only a receiver who hits the ground before he's had time for one must survive the
  ground. The rule now matches what people see, at the price of a judgment about time.
- **The order of events decides possession, and direction and territory decide the rest.** Ball out before
  the knee is a fumble; an NFL runner needs to be touched to be down. A forward fumble out of bounds comes back
  to the spot of the fumble, but into the opponent's end zone and out it's a touchback. A pass that doesn't go
  forward is a backward pass and stays live if dropped. Grounding is about the box and the line: once outside
  the box, a throwaway just has to reach the line.
- **Cameras measure, people spot**, and crew differences in flags are small and unstable from year to year.
